result.summary: Theseus's fame draws heroes to Calydon, where Diana's boar, sent in anger at Oeneus's neglect, is hunted and killed by Meleager and his band, including Atalanta. A quarrel over the spoils leads Meleager to kill his uncles, and his mother Althæa avenges them by burning the life-brand, so that he dies. His sisters mourn and are turned into birds.

scenes.title: Argument of the fable
scenes.summary: A prose summary of the Calydonian boar hunt, Meleager's death and his sisters' transformation.

scenes.title: Diana's anger at Œneus
scenes.summary: Athens celebrates Theseus, and Calydon asks his aid because Œneus omitted Diana from his offerings, so she sends a boar.
scenes.stakes: Calydon's harvest and people are threatened by Diana's vengeance.

scenes.title: The boar and the heroes
scenes.summary: The boar ravages crops and flocks until Meleager gathers a band of heroes, including Atalanta, with whom he falls in love.
scenes.stakes: The people's livelihood is lost unless the boar is stopped.

scenes.title: The hunt and the kill
scenes.summary: The boar kills and wounds several hunters. Atalanta wounds it first and Meleager kills it, then gives her the spoils.
scenes.stakes: Hunters risk death from the enraged boar.

scenes.title: Meleager kills his uncles
scenes.summary: The sons of Thestius seize the spoils from Atalanta and Meleager kills them in rage. Althæa learns of it and turns to vengeance.
scenes.stakes: Meleager risks his mother's wrath for his act.

scenes.title: Althæa burns the brand
scenes.summary: Recalling how the Fates tied Meleager's life to a billet, Althæa wavers and then burns it. Meleager dies in agony.
scenes.stakes: Meleager's life depends on the brand; Althæa is torn between son and brothers.

scenes.title: Mourning and the birds
scenes.summary: Calydon mourns, Althæa kills herself, and Diana turns Meleager's sisters into birds.
scenes.stakes: The sisters are lost in grief.

alias_notes.explanation: Atalanta is called by a name from Nonacris in Arcadia; the text also calls her Tegeæan.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable description of Atalanta's blend of boyish and girlish looks.
Terse observation that even gods feel wrath.
Althæa's anguished demand that Meleager return the life she twice gave him.

analysis.text: The passage shows divine wrath over neglected worship and a mother's conflict between kinship loyalties, leading to tragedy.
The hunt gathers many heroes of Greek legend, linking this tale to the Argonauts and later Trojan War figures.

legacy.text: The Calydonian boar hunt was a favourite subject of Greek and Roman art and of later European painting.

fun_facts.text: In Homer's version Meleager's death is not tied to a burning brand; the log motif appears in later tradition.

language_notes.text: Dædalus, the craftsman fleeing Crete, found refuge in Sicily with King Cocalus, who defended him against Minos. 'Ætnæan land' means Sicily, named for Mount Etna.
The 'mournful tribute' was the youths and maidens Athens sent to Crete to be devoured by the Minotaur; Theseus killed it and ended the payment.
Censers are vessels in which incense is burned during worship.
'Argive' and 'Achaia' here loosely mean Greek; the cities of Greece are meant, not only Argos.
'Palladian juice' is olive oil; Pallas is another name for Minerva, goddess of the olive.
'Daughter of Latona' is Diana; the poet names her by her mother instead of directly.
The line repeats itself (spikes, palisades, spikes) because the translator is rendering a Latin comparison closely; the bracketed numbers are the translator's footnote markers.
'Crops the expectations of the husbandman' means he destroys the farmer's hopes of a harvest by cutting down the young grain.
'Cæneus, now no longer a woman' alludes to the myth that Cæneus was born the girl Cænis and was changed into a man by Neptune.
The two sons of Tyndarus are Castor, the horseman, and Pollux, the boxer, the twin heroes also called the Dioscuri.
The father of Achilles is Peleus, here identified only by his famous son; the text's 'Telamon' is joined with him as a fellow hero.
'Against the will of the God' means Cupid, the god of love, makes him love her, though Meleager's fate is tied up with her presence.
'Vouchsafe' means to condescend or deign to grant something.
"Couples" are pairs of hounds leashed together; the hunters unleash them to start the chase.
The son of Ampycus is the seer Mopsus, who prays to Phœbus (Apollo), god of archery and prophecy.
"So far as he could" means Phœbus grants only half the prayer; Diana overrules the rest in the next sentence.
Nestor of Pylos later became the aged counsellor of the Greeks at Troy; the narrator notes he nearly died long before.
The two brothers are Castor and Pollux, the Gemini, later turned into the constellation; they ride white horses.
"Tegeæan damsel" is Atalanta, named from Tegea in Arcadia; "Nonacrian Nymph" and "Arcadian" also point to her region.
This Arcadian is Ancæus, who scorns Atalanta's hunting as unmanly.
The daughter of Latona is Diana, goddess of the hunt and protector of Atalanta.
The son of Ægeus is Theseus, speaking to his devoted friend Pirithoüs, son of Ixion.
The son of Æson is Jason, whose javelin misses the boar and kills a dog.
The three Sisters are the Fates, who spin and cut the thread of each life. They tie Meleager's lifespan to a burning piece of wood.
The narrator addresses Meleager directly as 'O youth' in the middle of the story.
The Eumenides (Furies) were goddesses of vengeance who punished crimes, especially against kin. Althæa invokes them to witness her act.
'Twice five months' is the ten lunar months of pregnancy, which Althæa cites as the cost of bearing her son.
Helicon is the Muses' mountain; a hundred tongues and the whole of Helicon is a traditional poet's wish for unlimited inspiration.
The daughter of Latona is Diana. Gorge and Deianira (daughter-in-law of Alcmena) were spared transformation; Deianira later marries Hercules.

context_notes.text: The Fates were said to have told Althæa that Meleager would live only until a certain brand burned away.
Ceres was goddess of grain, Bacchus of wine, Minerva of olives. First-fruit offerings thanked the gods for harvest.
Meleager is prince of Calydon, in Aetolia. The boar was sent by Diana to punish the country after its king neglected her in offerings.
Jason led the Argonauts on the ship Argo in the quest for the Golden Fleece; Theseus and Pirithoüs were famed friends.
Atalanta was a huntress from Arcadia, the only woman in this band of heroes. The Lycæan groves belong to Arcadia's Mount Lycæus.
The 'ivory keeper of her weapons' is a quiver made of or decorated with ivory, which holds her arrows.
Diana sent this boar to ravage Calydon because the king neglected her sacrifices, so she interferes to protect it.
The son of Œneus is Meleager, prince of Calydon and leader of the hunt.
Meleager, though the speaker, gives Atalanta the prize because he loves her. This gift later causes the quarrel with his uncles.
Plexippus and Toxeus are Meleager's maternal uncles. They were angry that he gave the boar's spoils to Atalanta.
Althæa is Meleager's mother and sister of the sons of Thestius, so the victims and the killer are both her kin.

literary_notes.text: Calling the boar Diana's 'servant and avenger' defines it as an instrument of divine wrath rather than an ordinary beast.
The short general maxim, echoing Virgil's famous question about divine anger, turns the particular slight into a universal truth about gods.
Comparing the boar to the largest bulls of Epirus and Sicily stresses its monstrous, unnatural size.
The boar's bristles are compared to spikes and palisades, making the animal seem like a fortified, armed wall.
Thunder from the boar's mouth and burning foliage from its breath exaggerate its monstrous, almost divine power.
Repeating 'in vain' stresses the farmers' helplessness and the emptiness of their waiting.
The balanced 'maid in a boy, boy in a maid' captures Atalanta's blend of femininity and masculinity.
Meleager's sudden love for Atalanta hints at the trouble that her presence will cause in the hunt and afterward.
The boar's charge is compared to lightning bursting from clouds, conveying sudden, violent force.
The boar is likened to a stone from a siege engine, magnifying its destructive power in heroic style.
The narrator looks ahead to the Trojan War, placing the mythic hunt within a larger heroic timeline.
Ancæus' boast of defying Diana and surpassing a woman prepares for his swift, gruesome death.
The boar's seizing of the boastful Ancæus is the punishment for pride, following directly on his vaunt.
Atalanta's pleasure in both gift and giver hints at her feeling for Meleager.
'Preserved' and 'had preserved' balance saving the billet against saving the son, and prepare the irony of destroying him.
The narrator turns to Meleager, 'O youth,' adding pathos and drawing the reader to his doomed fate.
Althæa's wavering is compared to a ship caught between wind and opposing tide, conveying her pull between two loyalties.
Althæa's repeated questions dramatize her inner conflict between maternal love and sisterly duty.
The billet seems to groan and the flames to resist, giving the object a life tied to Meleager's.
'Embrace it, and embrace it again' and the repeated kisses convey the sisters' unrestrained grief.
